transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-21
Start time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE); Maya (Redwood SE); Liam (Redwood CSM); Alicia (Head of Platform - HarborHealth); Marcus (NetOps); Priya (Security); Ethan (SRE)

Summary:
Short check-in for the Private POC: primary topics were bridgeback congestion under high egress, egress throttle tuning, and a flakey KMS handshake observed during key rotation. Agreed next steps include targeted replay of the handshake, a staging egress throttle experiment, and updated fallback thresholds.

Topics:
- Bridgeback backpressure: observed when bursts >1200 rps across canary
- Egress throttling and QoS shaping in customer VPC
- KMS handshake failures during rotation window (approx 1-2% error rate)
- Canary plan for alternate low-latency route and soak test
- Pricing/sizing for reserved burst capacity and fallback SLAs

Action items (also in metadata): see list above

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: ok hey everyone uh thanks for joining, let's do a quick round, uh intent for today is bridgeback pressure, K M S handshake weirdness and next steps for canary. Maya and I will start with notes from the runbook.
[00:28] Maya: yeah hi all, uh quick context - on Wednesday night we saw the canary spike, so the bridgeback path between HarborHealth VPC and our private nodes hit a backpressure condition, there's queueing and the p95 jumped, um about 420ms to 1.1s depending.
[00:47] Marcus: yeah that matches our telemetry, we saw tail latency and also an increase in retransmits on the tunnel, we suspected MTU and also a few jumbo frames being dropped, so we trimmed mtu and saw slight improvement.
[01:10] Priya: and we also correlate that with the key-rotation window where some calls failed, about 1-2% of the KMS API calls timed out, not sure if it's causally related.
[01:27] Ethan: quick question - are we sure the KMS is on the same route as the model traffic? I think our egress path for key ops differs.
[01:39] Maya: good call, so KMS calls go to the customer-managed KMS endpoint in us-west-2 via egress path A, model inference traffic goes via path B but the bridgeback is shared at a lower layer so congestion can affect both. It's messy.
[02:05] Jordan: yeah so the hypothesis is shared bottleneck at the transit gateway — when bursts hit >1.2k rps we exceed per-attachment bandwidth shaping and packets queue.
[02:22] Alicia: to add, our legal security asked for PSK handshake to be rotated daily, so the timeline aligns. We are worried about any dropped KMS calls during rotation windows, that's sensitive.
[02:38] Maya: that's fine, we can isolate handshake replay in staging. we'll turn on verbose TLS logs, capture the full TLS handshake and KMS client logs. we did an initial run and saw intermittent 503 from the KMS facade between 03:10 and 03:18 UTC.
[03:02] Marcus: yeah those 503s looked like backend overload in our metrics, not a Redwood bug necessarily, but the interplay is what matters.
[03:16] Jordan: important to note, Redwood has fallback that will route to a lower-cost model variant when latency rises, but that path still requires successful KMS decryption for sensitive tokens; if KMS fails we currently bubble an error to the caller. we probably want a graceful degrade that keeps non-sensitive traffic flowing.
[03:44] Priya: so we need a clear SLO: during key rotation, we can accept up to 0.5% KMS failures but we cannot accept data exfil risk. If fallback yields plaintext tokens cached, that's a no-go.
[04:05] Liam: noted. on the ops side, we recommended earlier a temporary cache TTL extension during rotations to reduce KMS pressure. worth testing.
[04:18] Maya: yes we tested TTL extension of KV cache to 30s from 5s and it reduced KMS QPS by about 18% in the spike window. but that increased memory usage slightly on the node.
[04:38] Ethan: memory increase is ok for staging, we want to see production effect. what's the impact on cost if we hold cache longer?
[04:47] Jordan: small increase in GPU memory footprint for the shard, doesn't change billing for hosted vs dedicated; in Dedicated you'd need to consider node sizing. but for the Private VPC pilot we can tune node config.
[05:02] Marcus: on egress throttle we did an experiment last night to shape at 900 rps per attachment, the p95 came down but overall throughput dropped and some requests were rejected upstream. it was a blunt instrument.
[05:20] Maya: right, shaping too conservatively causes upstream request queues to grow and results in 5xx for short periods. instead we recommended a burst token bucket with adaptive refill tied to queue depth, that preserves goodput under short bursts.
[05:39] Jordan: we have a patch that ties the token bucket to GPU queue depth, but it needs a small agent on the customer's side to report the queue depth metric. Marcus, is that feasible?
[05:50] Marcus: we can run the agent in staging yes, but need to vet it for security and resource usage. Priya will approve.
[06:02] Priya: yes I need the agent binaries and hash, plus a short threat model before we spin it up.
[06:12] Maya: understood, we'll provide the binary signed and the sha256, and a one-pager threat model.
[06:20] Jordan: good. next, on the KMS handshake flakiness — we think there are two failure modes: 1) actual KMS facade overload, 2) TLS session renegotiation hitting a library bug in our client version. we've got reproduction steps.
[06:38] Ethan: can you outline the repro?
[06:41] Maya: sure. in staging we simulate heavy inference traffic concurrent with a key rotation event. we then run the KMS client with debug enabled, pushing 1500 key-use ops per minute. the failure looks like a sub-second TLS timeout followed by a long tail. sometimes the client retries but gets bumped.
[07:02] Marcus: and we saw that if we stagger rotations across regions the failure disappears, which suggests a capacity transient.
[07:12] Jordan: action: Maya will replay the handshake logs across 4 pods and try with updated TLS library that includes a fix we have in internal branch. if the fix reduces flakiness we can propose an emergency micro release.
[07:30] Maya: i will also record pcap on the local interface to see if there's any fragmentation causing reassembly delays. sometimes Windows-ish jumbo frame mismatch results in odd behaviour, but that's likely not it.
[07:47] Alicia: one ask - can Redwood provide a fallback policy doc that lists order of routing fallbacks and how sensitive token failures are surfaced to the app? We need to show this to bizops.
[07:59] Liam: yes we will send an updated doc tonight with explicit step-down behavior: primary -> low-latency variant -> batch variant -> error with sanitized message. we'll note KMS-degraded state as a special case.
[08:15] Jordan: perfect. Now can we talk about canary plan for the alternate low-latency route? proposal is to run 10% traffic on the canary route for 6 hours, then 50% for 12 hours, with a 6-hour soak, checking p95, KMS error rate, and CPU.
[08:36] Ethan: 6-hour soak seems reasonable. i want an automatic rollback trigger if KMS error rate >0.8% or p95 > 800ms.
[08:48] Maya: agreed, we can wire those thresholds into the canary automation. we'll need to make sure circuit-breaker thresholds are aligned and make the rollback quick.
[08:58] Marcus: also consider transient errors during scheduled backup windows, we should avoid overlapping with our backup snapshot at 02:00 UTC.
[09:08] Jordan: scheduling note - we'll pick a window next week outside backups.
[09:12] Priya: quick question on encryption in transit for the bridgeback - are we using mTLS? I thought we were doing PSK.
[09:21] Maya: primary is mTLS for node <-> node, PSK for the transit gateway. we do mTLS between Redwood node processes and customer adapter. the PSK was for older regions, we are migrating.
[09:35] Priya: please add the mTLS cert rotation schedule to the doc.
[09:40] Jordan: will do.
[09:42] [10:00] Speaker 1: slight crosstalk here — uh sorry my mic popped, continue.
[10:06] Maya: back on throttle policy - we also recommended an adaptive egress throttle that exposes two knobs: burst window seconds and queue depth threshold. With these exposed you can change behavior without code deploy.
[10:24] Marcus: i'll take ownership of toggling the knobs during the canary, but need a one-click revert. can you add a runbook for that?
[10:33] Jordan: yes we'll include that in the runbook.
[10:36] Liam: pricing note — Jordan will send an estimate for reserved burst capacity; if HarborHealth wants a dedicated lane during peak windows that is priced separately.
[10:46] Jordan: i'll include options: (A) transient reserved burst credits, (B) dedicated Private lane with monthly commit.
[10:55] Alicia: likely we'd start with transient credits. lower risk.
[10:59] Maya: last technical item — kernel upgrade. we tested a small kernel bump on the nodes to resolve a scheduling issue; it reduced latency variance a touch but introduced a rare hang in the telemetry exporter. we've queued a patch for the exporter.
[11:20] Ethan: what's the hang frequency?
[11:22] Maya: about 0.01% in our stress runs, only on one kernel build. we'll hold rollout until we validate the exporter fix.
[11:32] Priya: we need to see the change log and CVE scan for that kernel before greenlighting in prod.
[11:40] Jordan: understood. we'll push the logs and CVE scan.
[11:45] Marcus: one last thing — can Redwood provide a short script to collect core metrics during the next spike? CPU, GPU queue depth, if possible the GPU utilization histogram.
[11:56] Maya: yes we have a small telemetry collector that we can provide as a container; we will sign it and include sha256 and a usage example.
[12:08] Jordan: ok recap — 1) Maya replay KMS handshake across 4 pods with TLS patch; 2) Marcus to run egress throttle experiment in staging and capture pcap; 3) Jordan sends pricing and canary scope; 4) Liam sends updated fallback doc; 5) Priya to validate agent and KMS key policy.
[12:32] Alicia: good; let's schedule next check-in for next Wednesday same time.
[12:36] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes and artifacts.
[12:40] [End of transcript]
